scope_allowed: Relevance of the quantities of interest

models.name: Model HF (High-Fidelity Composite Keel FEA)
models.what_it_computes: Nonlinear implicit 3D finite element simulation of the prosthetic foot keel and interface, computing load–deformation response, strain energy storage and release, hysteresis loss, and work-based energy return under prescribed gait- and sprint-like load histories.

models.name: Model RO (Reduced-Order Beam–Shell FEA)
models.what_it_computes: Parametric implicit finite element model using equivalent orthotropic shells and Timoshenko beams to approximate keel compliance and toe region contact, computing effective stiffness curves, stored/released elastic energy, and energy return for rapid design exploration.

mechanisms.name: M1: Mid-stance-to-toe-off elastic energy storage and return
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Determines user efficiency during level walking by quantifying the fraction of input work returned at toe-off, affecting metabolic cost and perceived responsiveness.

mechanisms.name: M2: High-rate push-off rebound during sprint initiation
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Captures rate-dependent energy return under fast loading, influencing propulsion and peak forces transmitted to the residual limb during athletic activities.

deviation.detail: Each credibility factor is scored per model–mechanism pair on a 0–9 numeric scale, where 0 indicates no substantiating evidence and 9 indicates convergent, multi-source evidence with traceable documentation; overall pair-level summaries are reported as the arithmetic mean of factor scores.

expected_decision.outcome_source: Within the decision context defined here, the assessed evidence supports continued use of the HF model for design substantiation in both mechanisms and judicious use of the RO model for walking-related screening.
rationale_keywords: close agreement with bench and in-shoe
underpredicted M2 returned work due to simplified rate dependence and contact

spans: The six-axis load cell at the anvil (capacity 5 kN, calibration uncertainty ±0.3%) and the pylon load cell (capacity 2 kN, calibration uncertainty ±0.3%) were calibrated within six months of the tests by an ISO/IEC 17025-accredited laboratory; the calibration certificates were archived with the test data.
Data management followed a documented procedure.
Reproducibility audits were conducted by re-processing 10% of the trials from raw signals to derived QoIs.

spans: Using Richardson extrapolation with an assumed second-order convergence rate for energy, we estimated an asymptotic value of 21.6 J, implying a relative error of 1.1% at the fine mesh.
Halving the nominal time increment from 5 ms to 2.5 ms and then to 1.25 ms at the fine mesh changed integrated work by 0.5% and the energy return percentage by 0.3 percentage points.

spans: Ply thickness measured from micrographs across five cross-sections averaged 0.180 ± 0.006 mm, aligning with the 0.18 mm per ply used in the model.

The friction coefficient between the toe region and anodized aluminum anvil was measured in a custom reciprocating rig under normal loads of 300–900 N and sliding speeds from 0.005 to 0.2 m/s, with mean mu = 0.68 ± 0.04.
The HF model used mu = 0.70 to fall within the measured range; the RO model used mu = 0.68 due to its Winkler foundation parameterization.

The vertical displacement of the pylon reference was prescribed to match the stance-phase displacement from motion capture averaged across participants for M1 and across sprint initiation trials for M2, appropriately scaled to the M26–M28 sizes by anthropometric normalization to foot length.
We verified that the resulting contact footprint in the HF model matched the pressure insole patterns to within 8% of area after morphological dilation to account for insole sensor spacing.
findings.span: Ply thickness measured from micrographs across five cross-sections averaged 0.180 ± 0.006 mm, aligning with the 0.18 mm per ply used in the model.

spans: The lamina properties used in the composite keel came from coupon tests manufactured with the same pre-preg lot and cure cycle as the tested keels.

The Prony term g1 and time constant tau1 were extracted from stress relaxation tests using a Prony series fit (R2 = 0.992 for compression, 0.987 for shear), which informed the implementation in both models.

Material laws, contact coefficients, and boundary histories were drawn from device-specific tests rather than tuned to match outputs, and their uncertainties were quantified to explain residual differences for both gait and sprint initiation conditions.
findings.span: The lamina properties used in the composite keel came from coupon tests manufactured with the same pre-preg lot and cure cycle as the tested keels.

spans: Physical test articles included six feet drawn from two production lots across sizes M26–M28.

In-shoe data came from nine unilateral transtibial prosthesis users (7 male, 2 female; 31–55 years; mass 70–88 kg; K3–K4 mobility) under IRB approval.
